newsitem.title: USA: UPS, union continue talks after brief recess.
newsitem.headline: UPS, union continue talks after brief recess.

text.p: Negotiators for United Parcel Service and the Teamsters union took a brief sleep break early on Sunday before resuming their marathon talks aimed settling the two-week old strike against the giant package delivery firm.

The two sides, who began their latest round of informal talks on Thursday morning at the urging of Labor Secretary Alexis Herman, had met for nearly 60 hours when they took a break at around 3:30 a.m. EDT (0730 GMT), a Labor Department spokesman said.

Herman canceled a scheduled appearance on a Sunday morning television talk show, but UPS Chief Executive Officer James Kelly, who has not been at the bargaining table, and Teamsters union President Ron Carey and were still scheduled to appear on other shows.

The department spokesman declined to say whether progress had been made in the talks, which are billed as informal, but said discussions would continue even while Carey was out of the Washington hotel where the two sides are encamped to appear on NBC's "Meet The Press."
A recorded message left by the union at 7 a.m. EDT (1100 GMT) said no agreements had been reached in any of the areas of the dispute that prompted a walkout by 185,000 UPS workers on Aug. 4.
"It is unclear whether progress will be made," the union recording said.
Herman, who was credited by Carey earlier with helping to keep the two sides talking, is planning to fly to Los Angeles on Monday morning for a speaking engagement.
Carey has announced plans for rallies in 30 U.S. cities on Thursday to drum up support for the strike. He said unions representing UPS workers in several European countries also planned job actions.
Buoyed by opinion polls showing the strikers winning the public relations battle, Carey has stuck to his theme that UPS convert more part-time jobs into higher paying full-time jobs.
CNN reported Saturday that a Gallup poll showed 55 percent of Americans backing the strikers.

A key issue for UPS, which has been urging union leaders to let their members vote on its so-called "last and final" offer, is to withdraw from its current multi-employer pension plan and set up a plan solely for Teamster members at UPS.

The strikers were getting help from other unions, but were finding it tough to live on $55-a-week strike benefits, while the company estimated $300 million in lost revenue a week, putting its losses so far at about $500 million or more.

UPS competitors, including the U.S. Postal Service, have rushed to try to fill the void. But many small businesses are feeling the pinch of being unable have their goods delivered by UPS, which has about 80 percent of the market share.

An Oklahoma lawyer announced on Saturday that he filed a federal lawsuit against UPS on behalf of a number of small and medium-sized companies, charging the shipper with breach of contract and negligence and seeking at least $75,000, the minimum required in federal court.
"Our cause of action is against UPS for negligence on the part of the management of UPS as well as breach of express and implied contracts," attorney Bob Joyner said.
President Bill Clinton has been resisting calls by UPS and some business groups to invoke the Taft-Hartley Act that would temporarily halt the strike.
